question: What was the primary focus of the original Universal Precautions introduced in the mid-1980s?

options.B: Bloodborne pathogens such as HIV and Hepatitis B

explanation: Universal Precautions were originally established by the CDC to protect healthcare workers specifically from bloodborne pathogens like HIV and Hepatitis B. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T8#GNS313_U2_T8_h1)

question: How do Standard Precautions differ from original Universal Precautions?

options.A: Standard Precautions apply only to surgical patients
options.B: Standard Precautions exclude contact with mucous membranes
options.C: Standard Precautions expand protection to include all body fluids, non-intact skin, and mucous membranes regardless of diagnosis
options.D: Standard Precautions are only used when a patient's infection status is confirmed as positive

explanation: Standard Precautions expanded on Universal Precautions to cover all body fluids (except sweat), non-intact skin, and mucous membranes for all patients regardless of status. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T8#GNS313_U2_T8_h1)

question: Why are Universal Precautions especially vital in resource-constrained Nigerian healthcare settings?

options.A: Diagnostic test results are always instantaneous
options.B: Infectious disease burdens are high and diagnostic testing may be delayed or unavailable
options.C: Nurses in Nigeria do not encounter bloodborne pathogens
options.D: Hospital-acquired infections do not occur in Nigeria

explanation: Because diagnostic testing may be delayed or unavailable, assuming every patient is potentially infectious protects nurses from high disease burdens without waiting for lab results. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T8#GNS313_U2_T8_h2)

question: What is a major benefit of treating every patient as potentially infectious?

options.A: It eliminates discriminatory practices and protects against undiagnosed infections
options.B: It reduces the total cost of hospital equipment
options.C: It removes the need for hand hygiene
options.D: It allows nurses to skip wearing gloves for minor procedures

explanation: Treating all patients equally prevents discrimination and ensures protection against infections that may not yet be diagnosed. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T8#GNS313_U2_T8_h2)

question: When should sterile gloves be used instead of non-sterile examination gloves?

options.B: For surgical interventions and invasive procedures like catheter insertion

explanation: Sterile gloves are required for surgical and invasive procedures to maintain asepsis, whereas non-sterile gloves suffice for routine physical assessments. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T8#GNS313_U2_T8_h3)

question: What is the recommended first step when removing (doffing) PPE to minimize self-contamination?

options.D: Wash the face shield while still wearing it

explanation: Gloves are typically the most contaminated item and are removed first during the doffing process, followed by hand hygiene or subsequent item removal. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T8#GNS313_U2_T8_h3)

question: According to the WHO 'My 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene', when should a nurse perform hand hygiene in relation to patient contact?

options.A: Only after finishing the entire shift
options.B: Before touching a patient and after touching a patient
options.C: Only when hands look visibly dirty
options.D: Before writing in the patient chart, but never before touching the patient

explanation: The WHO guidelines explicitly require hand hygiene both before touching a patient and after touching a patient, among other critical moments. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T8#GNS313_U2_T8_h4)

question: When is handwashing with soap and water strictly required over alcohol-based hand rub?

options.A: When hands are visibly soiled with blood or body fluids
options.B: Every time a patient room is entered
options.C: When taking a patient's temperature with a digital thermometer

explanation: Soap and water must be used when hands are visibly soiled with blood or body fluids because alcohol rubs do not effectively remove organic debris. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T8#GNS313_U2_T8_h4)

question: What is the recommended method for recapping a needle if it must be done?

options.A: Use a two-handed technique to quickly push the cap on
options.B: Hold the cap in one hand and push the needle directly into it
options.D: Ask a colleague to hold the cap while you push the needle in

explanation: The one-handed 'scoop' technique prevents the fingers of the non-needle-holding hand from being accidentally punctured. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T8#GNS313_U2_T8_h5)

question: At what level should a sharps disposal container be closed and replaced?

options.A: When it is completely packed to the absolute brim
options.B: When it reaches the designated fill line, typically three-quarters full
options.C: Once a month, regardless of how full it is
options.D: Only when needles start falling out of the top

explanation: Sharps containers must never be overfilled; they should be closed and replaced when reaching the fill line (about three-quarters full) to prevent needle-stick injuries. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T8#GNS313_U2_T8_h5)

question: Where should healthcare waste segregation take place?

options.A: At the incinerator site outside the hospital
options.B: At the point of generation immediately when waste is produced
options.C: In the general municipal dumping ground
options.D: By waste handlers at the end of the shift

explanation: Waste must be segregated immediately at the point of generation to prevent cross-contamination and protect all handlers. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T8#GNS313_U2_T8_h6)

question: What concentration of sodium hypochlorite (chlorine solution) is typically recommended for cleaning up blood spills?
explanation: A 0.5% sodium hypochlorite solution is the standard recommended strength for disinfecting surfaces contaminated with blood and body fluid spills. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T8#GNS313_U2_T8_h6)

question: What is the recommended immediate action after sustaining a needle-stick injury?

options.A: Squeeze the wound tightly and apply iodine
options.B: Wash the wound thoroughly with soap and running water
options.C: Ignore it if the patient appears healthy
options.D: Bandage the wound tightly without washing to trap the blood

explanation: Immediate first aid involves washing the injury site thoroughly with soap and running water without aggressive squeezing or scrubbing. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T8#GNS313_U2_T8_h7)

question: Within what timeframe should HIV Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) ideally be initiated for maximum effectiveness?

options.A: Within 2 hours, and no later than 72 hours
options.D: Only after laboratory confirmation of HIV transmission

explanation: HIV PEP is highly time-sensitive and should ideally be started within 2 hours of exposure, and not later than 72 hours, for a 28-day course. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T8#GNS313_U2_T8_h7)

question: What is a primary challenge community health nurses often face in Nigerian primary healthcare centers?

options.A: An overabundance of advanced surgical equipment
options.B: Basic infrastructure deficits such as lacking reliable running water and electricity
options.D: Excessive funding that is difficult to allocate

explanation: Primary health care centers in Nigeria frequently face infrastructural challenges like a lack of running water and electricity, requiring resourceful community nursing strategies. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T8#GNS313_U2_T8_h8)

question: How do community health nurses promote infection control compliance among local healthcare workers and traditional birth attendants?

options.A: By shutting down clinics that do not meet international tertiary standards
options.B: Through participatory education, training, and implementing context-appropriate safety practices
options.C: By forbidding anyone without a university degree from providing care
options.D: By relying solely on written policy manuals sent via mail

explanation: Community health nurses use participatory education and context-appropriate methods to train local workers and traditional birth attendants in safe practices. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T8#GNS313_U2_T8_h8)
